title: Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance - CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance - Bribery and Gratuities
subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: Which of the following would universally be considered an illegal kickback?
options: A vendor mailing a calendar with their logo on it to a buyer.
A vendor offering the agency an early-payment discount written into the contract.
A vendor secretly paying the buyer 2% of the contract value in cash in exchange for securing the award.
A vendor providing a standard volume-rebate check payable to the public agency.
questions.explain: A kickback is an illegal, secret payment made to a public official in return for a favorable contracting decision or for steering work to the vendor.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain I: Regulatory & Compliance

questions.q: While many agencies have a 'zero-tolerance' gift policy, some jurisdictions allow buyers to accept 'nominal promotional items.' Which of the following represents a nominal promotional item?
options: A $50 gift card to a steakhouse.
Tickets to a local professional baseball game.
An inexpensive coffee mug branded with the vendor's logo.
A weekend stay at the vendor's vacation property.
questions.explain: Nominal promotional items are inexpensive goods given widely for advertising purposes, such as cheap pens, mugs, or calendars bearing the company logo. Anything of notable monetary value (like tickets, vacations, or gift cards) is strictly forbidden.

questions.q: During the holiday season, a long-time vendor unexpectedly sends a large, expensive gift basket containing high-end electronics to the procurement manager's home. What is the most appropriate ethical action for the manager to take?
options: Keep it, since it was sent to their home and not the office.
Return the gift basket to the vendor with a polite letter explaining the agency's strict no-gift policy.
Distribute the electronics to the staff so one person doesn't benefit alone.
Donate the electronics to a local charity without notifying the vendor.
questions.explain: The most appropriate and defensible action is to return the prohibited gift directly to the sender alongside a formal note outlining the agency's ethics/gift policy. This makes the boundary clear to the vendor and creates a record of refusal.

questions.q: What is the primary legal distinction between a 'gratuity/gift' and a 'bribe'?
options: A bribe requires 'quid pro quo' intent to influence an official act, whereas a gratuity might lack explicit mutual intent.
A bribe is over $500 in value, while a gratuity is under $500.
Bribes are offered by vendors; gratuities are offered by citizens.
There is no legal distinction; the terms are synonymous in all criminal codes.
questions.explain: Bribery fundamentally requires corrupt intent—a 'quid pro quo' (this for that) to influence a specific official act. An illegal gratuity is a reward for a past or future official act but may not have the explicit 'I am paying you so you will do X' agreement of a bribe.

questions.q: A procurement professional attends an out-of-state conference. A prospective vendor offers to pay for the buyer's fancy dinner and a round of golf. Based on NIGP ethical guidelines, the buyer should:
options: Accept, because out-of-state conferences are exempt from local ethics laws.
Decline the offer, paying for their own meals and entertainment.
Accept, but only if they promise not to give the vendor a contract.
Accept, then report the cost to the IRS.
questions.explain: NIGP Code of Ethics strictly advises against accepting any gifts, meals, or entertainment from vendors or prospective vendors to avoid any appearance of impropriety or undue influence. Buyers should pay their own way.
